title: Take, Lord, receive
hook: Ignatius' prayer offering liberty, memory, understanding and will
carry: your love and grace are enough

segments.voice: Yesterday, rules for discernment. Your line was never decide in the dark. Did anything go up on the shelf for a calmer day? Day one thousand one hundred forty-eight.

The Spiritual Exercises end with an inventory. After praying through the life of Jesus, start to finish, Ignatius of Loyola asks the one praying to count up gifts: being made at all, being redeemed, and everything particular to their own life. Then he asks a question that sounds simple and isn't: given all that, what would you give back? His answer is a short prayer, known by its first word in Latin. Suscipe. Receive. It's today's word, and it closes our time with Ignatius.

Ignatius opens this last contemplation with two short notes about love. First, love shows itself more in deeds than in words. Second, love is a sharing: the one who loves gives what they have to the beloved, and the beloved gives back. Then comes the prayer. In plain English, it runs like this. Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my understanding, and my whole will, all that I have and possess. You gave it to me; to you, Lord, I return it. All of it is yours; do with it what you will. Give me your love and your grace; that is enough for me. Look at what's offered. Not money, not achievements. Freedom, memory, understanding, will: the inside of a person. And look at the reason. Paul asks the church at Corinth, in the King James: "what hast thou that thou didst not receive?" The Suscipe starts from that question. Nothing is handed over that wasn't a gift first. And the request at the end is small on purpose. Love and grace. Paul hears something like it from Christ: "My grace is sufficient for thee." That's where this week has been heading. We stepped into a gospel scene. We heard the king's call and stood between two banners. We kept watch at the cross and the empty tomb, learned to read the drift inside, and learned not to decide in the dark. It all ends here: not with a technique, but with a gift handed back. This is a hard prayer to mean all the way through. Some teachers of the Exercises call it a prayer to grow into, not a test to pass.
screen: `WHAT HAST THOU THAT THOU DIDST NOT RECEIVE?`
`A WEEK THAT ENDS WITH A GIFT RETURNED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the Suscipe, or sit with it. Settle, and let your breath slow. Go through the four slowly. Liberty: the freedom you have today. Memory: what you carry. Understanding: how you make sense of things. Will: what you choose. Pause on each. If you pray, you can say Ignatius' prayer, phrase by phrase, offering each one back. If you don't, simply hold each gift for a moment and notice where it came from. The bell holds the time.
Suscipe. Latin for receive: the first word of Ignatius' prayer offering liberty, memory, understanding and will, and asking only for love and grace.
Your line: your love and grace are enough. Today, when you catch yourself wanting more of something, say the line once and notice what's already been given. Day one thousand one hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: The Suscipe comes at the end of the Spiritual Exercises, in the Contemplation to Attain Love; Jesuits and others shaped by Ignatian spirituality pray it on retreat and in daily prayer, and it has been set to music as a hymn.

notes: The Suscipe is given as a close plain-English paraphrase of a real prayer, not quoted (no validator-listed public-domain translation); it is described and offered 'if you pray', not newly composed. Confirm the paraphrase is faithful.
The Latin text is understood to begin 'Suscipe, Domine'; confirm. Pronunciation given in ecclesiastical Latin.
The two notes on love (deeds more than words; love as mutual sharing) and the recollection of benefits (creation, redemption, particular gifts) paraphrase the Contemplation to Attain Love. Confirm.
'After weeks of praying' rests on the Exercises' four-week structure; confirm phrasing.
'Some teachers of the Exercises call it a prayer to grow into' is a soft attribution; confirm or cut.
howItsDone 'set to music as a hymn': settings exist (e.g. 'Take, Lord, Receive' by John Foley); confirm.
Week end (day 1148): the teach looks back over the week's Ignatian days; this is also the last day of the Ignatian way before the Celtic way begins.
